title: The verb in second place
goal: Master the most important word-order rule in Dutch: in a statement, the verb always sits in second place, whatever stands in front of it.
bekal: flip the sentence as soon as a time or place phrase comes first: *Morgen ga ik…*
order the rest of the sentence as time → manner → place
form yes/no questions and questions with a question word
wave: Review **Unit 8**: read ten random times off a clock at home, then turn each answer into the digital form.

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Wat doe je dit weekend?
dialogs.intro: Friday afternoon. Sanne is trying to make plans; Budi is trying to make sentences.

lines.speaker: Sanne:
lines.id: What are you doing this weekend?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Zaterdag ga ik naar Den Haag.
lines.id: On Saturday I'm going to The Hague.
lines.literal: Saturday go I to The Hague.

lines.speaker: Sanne:
lines.text: Leuk! Ga je met de trein?
lines.id: Nice! Are you going by train?
lines.literal: nice! go you with the train?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Ja, ik ga om negen uur met de trein naar het Mauritshuis.
lines.id: Yes, I'm taking the train to the Mauritshuis at nine.
lines.literal: yes, I go at nine hour with the train to the Mauritshuis.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Omdat ik het Meisje met de parel wil zien.
lines.id: Because I want to see the Girl with a Pearl Earring.
lines.literal: because I the girl with the pearl want see.

lines.speaker: Sanne:
lines.text: Dat schilderij is kleiner dan iedereen denkt.
lines.id: That painting is smaller than everyone thinks.
lines.literal: that painting is smaller than everyone thinks.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Dat zegt mijn tante ook altijd.
lines.id: That's what my aunt always says too.
lines.literal: that says my aunt also always.

lines.speaker: Sanne:
lines.text: En zondag? Doe je dan niets?
lines.id: And Sunday? Are you doing nothing then?
lines.literal: and Sunday? do you then nothing?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Zondag doe ik niets. Alles is dicht.
lines.id: On Sunday I'm doing nothing. Everything's closed.
lines.literal: Sunday do I nothing. everything is closed.

lines.speaker: Sanne:
lines.text: Niet meer, hoor. Maar rustig is het wel.
lines.id: Not anymore. But it is quiet, sure.
lines.literal: not more, you-know. but quiet is it indeed.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Dan slaap ik uit. Ook een plan.
lines.id: Then I'll sleep in. That's a plan too.
lines.literal: then sleep I out. also a plan.

notes: **Zaterdag ga ik naar Den Haag** — look at the order: time phrase first, then the **verb**, and only then the subject. In English this is impossible ("Saturday go I"), and that's exactly what you need to get used to.

**Omdat ik het Meisje met de parel wil zien** — in a subordinate clause, the verb is thrown to the **end** instead. The exact opposite of the rule above. That's Unit 20; for now, just notice that after *omdat*, *dat*, *als* the order changes.
**Netjes** (neat, tidy) is used as light praise for almost anything — a plan, handwriting, a piece of work.
**Het Meisje met de parel** — Vermeer's *Girl with a Pearl Earring*, on display at the Mauritshuis in The Hague. It measures 44 × 39 cm; almost every visitor is surprised by how small it is.
**Alles is dicht** — this used to be true: on Sundays the Netherlands was almost completely closed. Today many shops in big cities open (*koopzondag*), but in villages the old habit lives on.
**Dan slaap ik uit** — *uitslapen* means to sleep until you wake up on your own, with no alarm: to sleep in.
**Ook een plan** — a typical conversational fragment: "that counts as a plan too". Spoken Dutch loves clipping sentences like this.

grammars.title: The second-place rule
body: In a Dutch statement, **the main verb is always in second place**. Anything can stand in first place — the subject, a time phrase, a place, even the object. What gets pushed aside is the subject, which moves behind the verb.
after: Notice: the verb never moves. It's the subject that changes places. That's why this rule is called **inversie** — inversion. English has a trace of it in "Never *have I* seen…" or "Here *comes* the bus".

⚠️ The most common beginner mistake: *Morgen ik ga naar Amsterdam.* It sounds foreign to Dutch ears at once, even though the meaning is clear. Fixing it takes one habit: as soon as your sentence opens with anything other than the subject, swap the verb and the subject.
Remember the little rule from Unit 2: when *jij/je* moves behind the verb, its *-t* disappears. *Je gaat* → *Ga je?* / *Morgen ga je…*

grammars.title: The order of the rest: time, manner, place
body: After the subject and verb, the other parts of the sentence follow a fixed order, abbreviated **TMP**: *tijd* (time) → *manier* (manner) → *plaats* (place).
after: English prefers the reverse order: "I'm going to Utrecht by train tomorrow." A word-for-word copy of that habit will always sound wrong in Dutch.
TMP isn't a rigid law — any part can move up to first place for emphasis. What can never change is the verb's position.
The word *niet* (Unit 4) stands after time but before place: *Ik ga morgen **niet** naar Utrecht.*

blocks.text: Dutch questions come in two kinds, and both just move the verb.
1. Yes/no questions — the verb in FIRST place
2. Questions with a question word — question word first, verb second

blocks.title: Things to watch out for
items: *Welke* for de-woorden and plurals, *welk* for het-woorden: *welke bus*, *welk boek*.
*Waar … heen* and *waar … vandaan* split up in the sentence, just like separable verbs: *Waar kom je vandaan?*
Dutch has **no** helper verb for questions like English *do*. *Do you live here?* = *Woon je hier?* — just flip it.
⚠️ Intonation alone isn't enough to ask a question. *Je woont hier?* with a rising tone sounds like surprise, not an ordinary question.

sections.title: Linking words that don't change the order

blocks.text: These five linking words join two sentences **without** changing their word order at all. Other linking words (*omdat*, *dat*, *als*, *terwijl*) throw the verb to the end — that's for Unit 20.

head: Word
Meaning
Example
rows: Ik ga naar bed, **want** ik ben moe.
Het regent, **dus** ik neem de bus.

blocks.text: *Want* and *omdat* both mean "because", but they behave differently: after *want* the word order is normal, after *omdat* the verb is thrown to the end. *Ik blijf thuis, **want** ik ben ziek* = *Ik blijf thuis **omdat** ik ziek **ben**.* For now, use *want* — it's always safe. (⚠️ False friend: *want* doesn't mean "want"!)
*Dus* at the start of a sentence triggers inversion like any other opening phrase: *Het regent. **Dus neem** ik de bus.*

exercises.prompt: Rewrite each sentence with the bold part in first place.
Put the parts in the right time-manner-place order.

items: ____ ga je niet mee? (ik ben moe)
